title: Grade 8 Integrated Science Scheme of Work: Forces and Motion (Synthetic Mock Corpus)
subject: Integrated Science

entries.topic: Forces and motion: Types of forces, newtons and weight
priorKnowledge: A force is a push or a pull
learningOutcomes: Classify forces as contact or non-contact and give an example of each
Measure force in newtons using a newtonmeter
Calculate weight using weight = mass x gravitational field strength with g = 10 N/kg
keyConcepts: contact forces: friction, tension, air resistance, upthrust
non-contact forces: gravity, magnetic force, electrostatic force
mass is the amount of matter in kg and does not change with location
weight is the force of gravity on a mass, measured in newtons
learningActivities: Learners sort force cards into contact and non-contact
Learners measure the weights of classroom objects with newtonmeters and calculate each mass using g = 10 N/kg
Learners compare predicted and measured values and discuss differences
Learners draw force arrows on pictures showing weight and contact force
entries.assessment: Calculate the weight of a 3 kg bag on Earth using g = 10 N/kg and state why its mass would be unchanged on the Moon.
entries.teacherNotes: Learners often use 'weight' and 'mass' interchangeably in everyday speech. Use g = 10 N/kg as a rounded value (it is about 9.8 N/kg on Earth) and about 1.6 N/kg on the Moon. Note that mass stays constant but weight changes with gravitational field strength.

entries.topic: Forces and motion: Balanced and unbalanced forces
priorKnowledge: Force arrows show the size and direction of forces
learningOutcomes: Draw force diagrams and determine the resultant force on an object
Explain that balanced forces produce no change in motion and unbalanced forces change speed or direction
Describe the effect of friction on moving objects
keyConcepts: balanced forces have a resultant of zero
unbalanced forces cause acceleration, deceleration or change of direction
an object at rest or moving at constant speed in a straight line has balanced forces
learningActivities: Learners play tug-of-war with ropes to compare equal and unequal pulls
Learners pull a trolley using hanging masses over a pulley and describe the motion for different masses
Learners draw force diagrams for a book on a table, a car at constant speed and a car braking
Learners calculate the resultant force for given one-dimensional force pairs
resources: Trolleys, pulleys, string and slotted masses
entries.assessment: A car moves at a constant speed with a driving force of 800 N. State the size of the resistive forces and explain.
entries.teacherNotes: A common difficulty is the belief that a force is needed to keep an object moving at constant speed. Show that constant speed requires balanced forces. Learners also think that no motion means no forces act; stationary objects still have balanced forces acting. Draw arrows to scale where possible.

entries.topic: Forces and motion: Speed, distance and time
learningOutcomes: Calculate speed using speed = distance / time with units m/s and km/h
Describe the motion of an object from the shape of a distance-time graph
keyConcepts: gradient of the line represents speed
horizontal line means the object is stationary
learningActivities: Learners time a toy car or a walking learner over a measured 10 m course and calculate speed
Learners plot a distance-time graph from collected data
Learners match distance-time graphs to descriptions of journeys
Learners solve speed problems that include unit conversion between m/s and km/h
resources: Metre rules or trundle wheel, stopwatches
entries.assessment: A cyclist travels 600 m in 120 s. Calculate the average speed and describe what a horizontal section on the distance-time graph means.
entries.teacherNotes: Learners often read a distance-time graph as a picture of the path or think a horizontal line means constant speed; it means the object is stationary. A steeper line means a higher speed. To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6.
